abstract: This monograph addresses the optimal selection of equipment for chemical-engineering systems of multiproduct batch plants, a large-scale NP-hard discrete optimization problem in which, for each processing stage, a unit of standard size must be chosen so that the total capital cost of the equipment is minimized while the system remains operable and produces the required products within a given time horizon. We present the mathematical model of system operation and analyze its computational properties. We then develop a sequential branch-and-bound algorithm and its parallel versions for shared-memory systems (OpenMP), distributed-memory clusters (MPI, master-worker), and graphics processing units (CUDA), including recursive and iterative tree traversal, shared-memory optimization, and branch-divergence reduction. To overcome the exponential growth of the run time, we propose a hybrid metaheuristic in which Ant Colony Optimization finds a feasible initial solution and Simulated Annealing improves it, and we implement it on GPUs with thousands of independent threads. Finally, we propose random, constant, and multi-constant approaches to tuning the parameters of the ant colony algorithm based on statistical analysis of many parallel runs, and we study the program on GPUs of three generations and on nodes with several GPUs. Computational experiments on multi-core processors, clusters, and GPUs show that the parallel hybrid algorithm finds solutions within 0.01% of the branch-and-bound optimum in tens of seconds instead of tens of hours.

title: Decisions at the end of the world
author: Casper van Elteren
abstract: International treaties are often described as tigers without teeth, failing to secure compliance or change outcomes. Cooperation also depends on how states maintain the rules they have already made -- especially where no sovereign stands above the states. Here we map more than six decades of decision-making under the Antarctic Treaty, linking submitted proposals to recorded responses and tracing how instruments act on earlier ones. Shared references tie decisions together across the agenda. Recurring revision concentrates in specialised histories, above all the management of protected areas, beyond what activity, popularity and reference age predict. Periodic administrative reviews retire outdated instruments in bulk, joining otherwise separate histories without coordinating policy across subjects. Binding Measures build overwhelmingly on earlier Measures, with little direct succession from non-binding Resolutions. Distinguishing these layers shows how a shared rule system is sustained by consensus, and provides a basis for comparing cooperation across global commons.

title: Low Language Transfer Speech-to-Text
author: Husein Zolkepli
abstract: A multilingual speech recogniser has heard much speech in its own languages. We ask how much of that it brings to a language it was never trained on, when it is fine-tuned on the little that language has. We score 28 open multilingual models untouched on Low-Language-TTS, 50 low-resource languages in 11 writing systems, and fine-tune 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips a language, 82 hours in all, with a dev set choosing every epoch. Fine-tuning lowers every model's macro character error rate (CER), by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best, and a word language model takes three CTC models 1.2 to 1.4 points lower; WER is still 34.4 at best. On the 12 languages that no model lists, every model starts at 46 or worse and the best ends at 11.7. The same architectures from random weights stay 60 points or more behind, so the gain is transfer, and an encoder left untouched already gives a Whisper or Qwen decoder most of what it needs. It is the language, not the corpus: on FLEURS recordings that ours do not share, the median model keeps 79% of its gain. It costs the languages the models knew, 5.7 points of CER on English, Spanish, French and German in the median model. Low-rank adapters on 4% of the weights come within 1.1 points of tuning everything, and on 2 of 3 models forget less. Seq2seq and language-model decoders are done within three to five epochs, while a new CTC head is still improving at twenty or thirty. Data beats epochs: 25 clips a language take Qwen3-ASR 0.6B from 60.9 to 39.3, and at equal clips presented, ten times the data is worth 9.7 points. A model that first learned forty of the languages learns the other ten no faster. On a public Malay benchmark, untouched Whisper large-v3 scores 8.9 when it detects the language and 14.9 when told the clip is Malay, because it then translates the English that speakers mix in; trained on the Scicom telephony dataset it scores 6.0.

title: BWM-Forge: Agentic World Programming for Embodied Intelligence
author: BWM Team
abstract: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.

title: Guided Generation of Linux Kernel Semantic Patches with Small Local Language Models
author: Mohanned Ahmed
abstract: When a Linux kernel API changes, hundreds of drivers are converted by hand over months, and the earlier conversions are reviewed examples for the later ones. We ask whether small open language models running on a laptop can turn such examples into Coccinelle semantic patches, the rules kernel maintainers already use for tree-wide changes. We adapt guided code generation to this task: the training examples are decomposed by script into a tree of change variants, the model writes one small rule per variant under feedback from applying it to the examples, deterministic components repair SmPL syntax and generalise driver-specific names, rules are composed greedily, and a compile critic repairs or rejects a rule whose output does not build. We evaluate on a pre-registered test set of 7 migrations whose new APIs appeared after the training cutoffs of all three models (Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 4B), with 122 held-out driver conversions, counting a conversion as solved only if the rule's output matches the human fix and compiles. With the framework, Qwen2.5-Coder solves 35.3 conversions on average over three seeds (range 32-41), against 1.0 when prompted directly; Spinfer solves 41 and a frontier LLM agent 66. The local model solves fewer conversions than Spinfer but its rules are the most precise on the test set (0.74 of the files they change are solved, against 0.55 for Spinfer and 0.70 for the frontier agent), and the compile critic removes every output that matches the human fix but does not build. The two general-purpose models stay weak even with guidance (at most 12 solved). All code, prompts, model responses and results are released.

title: An Agentic Python Framework for LLM-Driven UVM Testbench Synthesis with Closed-Loop Compiler Feedback
author: Vikash Kumar
abstract: Protocol bridge verification is a persistent bottleneck in SoC development: for every new bridge instance, engineers hand-craft a full UVM testbench from scratch, consuming 40--100 engineering hours of bring-up effort. We present an agentic Python framework that generates complete, protocol-aware UVM testbenches for arbitrary IP and subsystem configurations from a structured Verification Manifest---a JSON specification encoding interface topology, protocol semantics, and coverage intent. The framework employs a dual closed-loop architecture: an inner compiler feedback loop that injects categorised UVM diagnostics rather than raw tool output, and an outer coverage loop driven by intent-gap analysis against the Manifest. Validated on the AMBA AHB-to-APB bridge---a representative production protocol bridge with a 7-state control FSM, two-phase APB handshake, and non-trivial burst serialisation logic---the framework achieves 96.8% functional coverage, a $4.7\times$ bring-up speedup, and a Protocol Verification Completeness score of 0.87, with only 2.1% of the generated 4,623-line testbench requiring human correction. The generated scoreboard independently identified a critical RTL functional fault that the manual baseline missed entirely. Generalisation across four protocol families confirms that speedup increases with protocol complexity, ranging from $3.1\times$ (APB Subordinate) to $6.1\times$ (CHI Subordinate).

title: Weak Composition Theorems for Randomized Communication
author: Pachara Sawettamalya
abstract: We present two results towards the randomized communication complexity of composed functions. Our contributions include: - \textbf{Lifting-by-Influence.} For any binary function $f$ and any outer gadget $g:\{0,1\}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, we show that up to additive terms, computing $g \circ f^n$ information-theoretically requires solving at least $\operatorname{Inf}(g)$ instances of $f$, where $\operatorname{Inf}(g)$ denotes the total influence of $g$. To our knowledge, this is the first composition lower bound for randomized communication that applies to \emph{every} choice of $f$ and $g$. - \textbf{Symmetric Composition.} When $g$ is a symmetric function with a value transition at Hamming weight $d$, we strengthen the number of required instances to $\min\{d,n+1-d\}$. As an implication, this recovers the previously known direct-sum theorem, XOR lemma, and majority lemma. Our proofs develop novel and distinctive usages of the classical \emph{input embedding} argument of Barak, Braverman, Chen, and Rao (SICOMP 2013). As an additional ingredient, we introduce a new public sampling framework that avoids auxiliary communication during the recovery phase of the protocol, ultimately reducing the extra cost from $O(n)$ bits of information to just $O(1)$.

title: Same-State Pairs Make One JEPA Proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis Vacuous
author: Xin Li
abstract: In a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), the JEPA proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) assumes that every observation determines the world state and that a spectral gap makes minimizers unique up to rotation. Under the hard-whitening population objective, same-state positive pairs make the induced world kernel the identity: every centered whitened state function is a global minimizer, and, when $d_z-1\ge 2k$, two minimizers can have best-rotation squared residual $2k$. The uniqueness claim is conditional; for $k<d_z-1$, where $d_z$ is the number of world states, this limit makes its premise unsatisfiable, so the claim has no content there. The experiments that motivate it leave the assumption: a caption sees only part of an image, and the paper states no experiment meets its hypotheses exactly. The theorem does not reach those experiments, and for $k<d_z-1$ its idealized same-state limit is vacuous. One of the paper's four quantitative results survives: a gap-free lower bound. Its bound vanishes only at perfect scene-explained fraction; it bounds alignment error but cannot certify good-view alignment. A canonical frame is determined only up to a rotation and a latent permutation. Paired samples fix the relative frame at effective rank $k$; a global rotation remains. Component semantics fix the relative permutation only up to signs; value anchors fix it once the mixing frame is pinned. A resource--gauge ledger records which resource fixes which gauge.

title: A One-Sided Sublinear-Query Tester for Bounded-Degree 2SAT
author: Yuichi Yoshida
abstract: We give a one-sided tester for satisfiability of 2CNF formulas in the bounded-degree model. For every degree bound $Δ$, distance parameter $\varepsilon>0$, and $ν\in(0,1/2)$, its query complexity on $n$-variable formulas is $\widetilde O_{\varepsilon,Δ,ν}(n^{1/2+ν})$.

title: SwarmSafe-Delta: Isolating Message Effects on LLM Agent Safety
author: Junru Zhu
abstract: When a tool-using LLM agent team violates policy, aggregate outcomes do not reveal whether an upstream message changed the executor's action. We introduce SwarmSafe-Delta, a paired executable protocol that freezes upstream computation, varies real, hidden, and format-matched placebo delivery, and scores a single committed action against deterministic benign and risky policy states under preassigned budgets. Across four models and constructed optional tasks, real delivery at $N=4$ produces 21.4% risky-world violations, versus 5.0% with placebo and 1.0% with hidden delivery (paired differences +16.4 and +20.3 percentage points). Real delivery also improves benign task success, illustrating that suppressing communication sacrifices utility. In a second regime constructed to require an upstream lookup route, real delivery improves safe completion by 74.2 points relative to hidden delivery. These effects quantify message-delivery contrasts under specified information dependencies, not naturally occurring failure rates. Exploratory action-level analyses show that the effect depends strongly on whether the upstream message recommends a prerequisite check or direct execution; model differences also largely track these message compositions. The contribution is a controlled, execution-grounded measurement protocol rather than a general claim that agent communication is harmful or protective.

title: Optimal Additive Integer Masks for One-Guess Vulnerability under an Absolute-Moment Budget
author: Joonas Pääkkönen
abstract: We study the average one-guess success probability of an adversary who observes the ordinary integer sum of a finite-support secret and an independent integer-valued mask, subject to an absolute-moment budget on the mask. For a uniform secret on an interval the exact optimum and an explicit optimiser are obtained. For a biased bit the masks that achieve no increase over the prior baseline are characterised and their minimal cost is determined. The entire cost-vulnerability frontier is then determined for every bias. It is the piecewise-linear interpolation of an explicit sequence of points generated by cost-optimally shifted truncated geometric masks. It has infinitely many affine pieces, which accumulate at the critical cost, where the frontier meets the prior baseline with zero slope. The proof rests on a layer-cake decomposition of an arbitrary mask into truncated geometrics, along which both the vulnerability and the cost are exactly additive. The results give exact design guidance for additive integer noise under the average one-guess metric; they do not constitute a cryptographic masking scheme.

title: Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation as an Optimization Constraint for Continual Learning
author: Davide Wiest
abstract: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is a widely used regularization-based technique for continual learning, protecting performance on old tasks with a quadratic penalty whose empirical Fisher is usually justified through probabilistic curvature. We instead introduce Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC): new training must preserve chosen functionals of learned behavior. EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each sample's loss. This derivation exposes a flaw: EWC implicitly weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so well-fitted samples lose importance. EWC-DR observed this failure in classification; CLOC identifies its general cause. Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation (IEWC) penalizes output changes according to the first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, removing the weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry, and prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, uniform IEWC improves ImageNet-R accuracy over matched EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07).

title: Continual Event Recognition for Autonomous Optical Network Monitoring
author: Khouloud Abdelli
abstract: Autonomous optical networks require monitoring systems capable of adapting to evolving disturbances without repeated retraining or service interruption. We propose a continual event recognition framework for state-of-polarization (SOP)-based optical monitoring based on prototype representations, open-set recognition, and few-shot prototype registration. The framework supports recognition of known disturbances, detection and integration of novel events, and investigates whether overlapping disturbances can be inferred through compositional reasoning from existing prototypes. Experimental validation on a 2600-km ROADM-based optical testbed demonstrates 99.82% closed-set recognition accuracy, successful adaptation to novel disturbances without encoder retraining, and reveals that overlapping optical disturbances exhibit varying degrees of latent compositionality. While some overlaps can be recognized in a zero-shot manner through prototype composition, others require explicit few-shot registration. These results establish continual event recognition as a promising paradigm for future autonomous optical network monitoring systems.

title: A Unified Interpretable Semantic Framework for Multi-Modal Fiber Sensing Under Data Scarcity
author: Khouloud Abdelli
abstract: We propose a unified interpretable semantic framework for multi-modal fiber sensing under data scarcity. The framework maps heterogeneous measurements from state of-polarization (SOP) monitoring, distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), and optical time-domain reflectometry (OTDR) into a shared set of physics-grounded semantic descriptors capturing impulsiveness, persistence, structural characteristics, and energy concentration. Inference is performed through reasoning over semantic class profiles, optionally assisted by retrieval of semantically similar examples to resolve ambiguity and support adaptation without model retraining. Experimental validation on real SOP, DAS, and OTDR datasets demonstrates robust performance across sensing modalities, achieving accuracies of 95.0%, 91.1%, and 94.6%, respectively, while providing transparent and physically interpretable decisions. The proposed framework establishes a unified and data efficient approach for optical fiber sensing in evolving and data scarce deployment environments.

title: Adaptive Distance Detection and Adaptive Instance Segmentation
author: Kai Yi Ji
abstract: This paper is about object detection model and semantic segmentation model in an FPS game Counter Strike: Condition Zero to detect enemies. Semantic segmentation is pixel-wise detection algorithm. We customized the architecture for semantic segmentation. We used YOLOv5s to train object detection model. After training, the inference time of semantic segmentation was compared to object detection. It was observed that object detection was slightly faster and semantic segmentation is slower but better at detecting the exact shape of the object. However, we found out that this slight difference of inference can grow exponentially if the both models get more complex. To solve this, we propose a novel approach called Adaptive distance detection which combines both algorithms. We will also introduce Adaptive instance segmentation to combine semantic segmentation and panoptic segmentation.

title: PhysICL: In-Context Learning of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes from Procedural Priors
author: Fabien Casenave
abstract: Engineering design studies produce a few tens to a few hundred simulations of one problem, each on its own mesh, and their surrogates are retrained for every study. Tabular foundation models instead infer a new task from its examples in one forward pass, after pretraining on synthetic tasks. We demonstrate the feasibility of in-context learning for physical field prediction on unstructured meshes. A single model, PhysICL, pretrained solely on procedural tasks, predicts fields, with quantiles, directly on each query mesh from labeled simulations, without updating its weights. The same checkpoint accepts variable numbers of context examples, scalar inputs and input fields, and any number of output fields, while mesh size and connectivity can vary within a task. Its procedural prior draws generic laws and boundary-element physical models on morphed 2D and 3D template meshes, evaluated only at the points the model samples, fast enough that tasks generated on the fly by CPU workers keep the GPUs busy throughout pretraining. On five PLAID datasets never seen in pretraining, its field error decreases as the context grows and, from $K = 32$, is below that of the nearest context simulation on every dataset and context draw. It is on par with per-dataset reduced-order models on two of them, behind them where the fields are low-rank. On AhmedML surfaces with a median of 1.1 million nodes, twenty times the largest pretraining mesh, its fixed spatial budgets keep the peak GPU memory at $K = 64$ at 4.27 GiB, against 4.07 GiB on the 6,000-node meshes of 2D\_MSHE. Finally, on 2D\_MSHE, far from the prior, fine-tuning on procedural tasks that reproduce its geometry and loads, without any of its outputs, at a tenth of the pretraining cost, divides the stress error by 2.7.

title: The Distributed Run Manager A C++ Library for Distributed Processing
author: Brian Harrawood
abstract: The DistributedRunManager (DRM) is a C++ library for distributing a computing task among a number of computer systems for parallel processing on a network. The library was originally designed to accelerate synthetic image production for tomographic images, but is also a general solution for distributing a software task across diverse, multiple hardware platforms. The DRM self-configures using a novel C++ class, the ElectionManager. This class selects a server cooperatively at runtime and eliminates the need for a priori distribution configuration. All communication, logging, and fault-tolerance mechanisms are encapsulated by the DRM, providing a "black-box" interface to the application developer.

title: Owned Edits to a Shared Decision Rule: Learning Private Exceptions as Typed, Gated, Withdrawable Weight Edits
author: John J. O'Hare
abstract: Organisations that apply the same published decision rule often hold private evidence that the rule is wrong for their own cases, and will not pool it. We describe a learning mechanism for that setting whose unit of change is an owned edit. The published rule is compiled exactly into a small ReLU network, a structured prior. Each party's learner searches a small typed space of declarations, a few named values such as subject, scope, form and size, and proposes one only when its own records pass a selection-aware evidence gate. The learning is that gated search around the prior. In two analyses registered before they ran, on synthetic data with 20 sampled hidden truths, the learner at 30 records per party was non-inferior, within 2 points, to all seven tuned baselines (a confined gradient learner, Ditto, FedRep, federated averaging, two pooled networks and pooled gradient-boosted trees), scoring 96.6% against 91.7% for the unchanged rule; the same search without the prior or the gate scored 84.0%. In a third registered test, typed edits over a network trained on shared records beat that network alone by 5.4 points and the same edits over the published rule by 3.1. An acceptance body recomputes each edit from its declaration and writes it into units reserved for that party, so by construction an edit changes no decision about any other subject, withdraws exactly, discloses at most log2 of the typed space's size in bits, and can hide nothing beyond its declared values. We report where it loses: truths shared by all parties, relaxations, ten records, a pre-stated gate criterion that failed in both runs, and a language model given the records that decided about as accurately on one draw. On a rule-only base, a table of owned exceptions makes the same decisions.

title: Sharp Lower Bounds for Parallel Log-Concave Sampling
author: Evan Dogariu
abstract: How many rounds of parallel queries are needed to sample from a smooth, strongly log-concave distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$? For every fixed condition number $κ\in (1, \infty)$, we prove that any sampler making polynomially many queries per round requires $Ω_κ(\log d)$ rounds to achieve constant total variation error in the worst case. The lower bound holds even if queries return derivatives of all orders. Together with the first-order parallel Picard algorithm of \cite{zhou2025parallel}, this establishes a depth complexity of $Θ_κ(\log d)$ for parallel log-concave sampling with $\operatorname{poly}(d)$ width. We then study centered Gaussian targets to understand how much width is needed at a given depth. From \cite{chewi2023query,zhou2026complexitygaussiansampling}, it is known that either one round of width $d$ or $\mathcal{O}(\sqrtκ \log d)$ rounds of constant width suffice for first-order Gaussian sampling. At fixed $κ$ we characterize the depth-width tradeoff interpolating between these regimes: when using $ \lceil c \log d\rceil$ rounds, if $0 < c < c_\star(κ)$ then the optimal width at constant TV error is $\widetildeΘ(d^{1-c/c_\star(κ)})$, while if $c \geq c_\star(κ)$ then it is $Θ_κ(1)$. Here, $c_\star(κ)$ is an explicit constant with $c_\star(κ) \sim \sqrtκ / 8$ as $κ\to \infty$.

title: k-partite quantum homomorphisms
author: Amin Karamlou
abstract: $k$-partite XOR games and linear binary constraint system (BCS) games arise from systems of linear equations over $\mathbb{Z}_2$, providing distinct quantum relaxations of the same classical constraint satisfaction problem (CSP). Linear BCS games have been generalised to synchronous homomorphism games on arbitrary relational structures, with compositional semantics provided by the quantum monad. We introduce $k$-partite homomorphism games, extending $k$-XOR games from linear systems to arbitrary relational structures. This yields a framework for studying multipartite quantum CSPs and quantum homomorphisms. We characterise perfect strategies in both the tensor-product and commuting-operator models as Kleisli morphisms of suitable state-dependent graded quantum monads on a category of $k$-partite relational structures. We then study quantum advantage in the pseudotelepathic sense: the existence of a perfect quantum strategy without a perfect classical strategy. We show that synchronous and $k$-partite quantum advantage are incomparable at the level of CSP instances. The GHZ instance admits three-player quantum advantage but no synchronous commuting-operator advantage, whereas the magic-square instance admits synchronous quantum advantage but no $k$-partite commuting-operator advantage for any number of players or proper colouring. We also exhibit an explicit six-element template whose CSP is NP-complete and admits two-player quantum advantage. Finally, we prove that no bounded-width CSP template admits $k$-partite quantum advantage, even in the commuting-operator model.

title: Rule-Sensitive Sensor Participation in Distributed Detection with Prescribed Boolean Fusion Rules
author: Ahmad Tanha
abstract: We study distributed binary detection when the fusion node must implement a prescribed Boolean decision rule. Under conditionally independent Bernoulli observations, we derive a signed-influence path identity valid for arbitrary Boolean rules; for monotone rules, it reduces to an exact Russo--Margulis representation in terms of coordinate influences. The identity yields rule-sensitive necessary conditions for a target Bayes error and an influence-weighted Kullback--Leibler feasibility bound. We then connect Boolean relevance to exact rule implementation and derive lower bounds on the number of sensors that must participate, including a heterogeneous bound based on the ordered per-sensor hypothesis separations. Numerical and Monte Carlo results illustrate both the tightening provided by the heterogeneous participation bound and the performance penalty that can arise when a prescribed fusion rule is retained instead of optimal likelihood-ratio fusion.

title: On Multi-Constrained Path Finding utilizing Grover Search and Decoded Quantum Interferometry
author: Dmitrii Chemodanov
abstract: Finding a path whose totals under several additive metrics all fall inside prescribed ranges is weakly NP-complete. We ask what two quantum algorithms can do for it, against strong classical baselines. For directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) we give a Grover search whose state preparation builds the uniform superposition over all source-to-destination paths with one qubit per arc and no ancilla. We prove it correct, give its exact gate count, and show that measured strings form an error- detecting code whose distance is a girth-like graph parameter. We complete the oracle and count its gates: one search on our largest instance, 136 arc qubits and 262,144 paths, needs about 4.4 x 10^5 Toffoli gates, while classical dynamic programming decides the same instance with 18,754 labels. Grover search needs O(sqrt(N/M)) oracle calls for M good paths among N . Classical meet-in-the-middle matches this exponent in the worst case, and known quantum algorithms with quantum memory beat it. For a staged fabric with node-independent linear weights, maximizing the number of satisfied metrics is max-LINSAT, and with power- of-index weights it is Optimal Polynomial Intersection, where no known polynomial-time classical algorithm matches decoded quantum interferometry (DQI). We verify this translation in simulation and run two small binary instances on IBM Heron processors, which keep 67 % and 15 % of the ideal gain over uniform sampling.

title: Bounded Knapsack in Truly Subquadratic Time
author: Huanyi Zhou
abstract: Bounded Knapsack asks how many copies of each item to take to maximize profit under a capacity constraint. Given $n$ records with binary-encoded multiplicities, we return optimal counts in randomized time with a fixed power saving in the maximum item weight $w_{\max}$ or maximum item profit $p_{\max}$. Fix $1<ρ<2$ and suppose integer $(\min,+)$-convolution on length-$m$ arrays can be computed with failure probability at most $η$ in $\widetilde O(m^ρ)$ time, up to polynomial factors in the entry bit length and $\log(1/η)$. Put $f(ρ)=4(3-ρ)/(8-3ρ).$ For any fixed $ε>0$, on inputs whose integers have magnitude polynomial in $n+\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})$, our algorithm runs in time $$\widetilde O\bigl(n\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})^{f(ρ)+ε}\bigr).$$ It returns optimal counts with high probability. If convolution saves $δ=2-ρ$ in its exponent, knapsack retains $δ/(1+3δ/2)$. With the integer convolution exponent $1.9601397040925$, a separate parameter choice gives $\widetilde O(n+\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})^{1.961})$, including for 0-1 Knapsack. We keep the copies compressed. Witnessed convolutions generate residual queries, and local linear programs filter them by cost. Resilient lattice cores allow recursive states to coalesce. Progression reserves support rounding, and a thin affordable fiber yields a lift that reduces the normalized column volume. This volume bounds the number of LP regions a grid lookup examines.

title: Multiple-Choice Knapsack with Small Items
author: Jakub Pawlewicz
abstract: The Multiple-Choice Knapsack problem is a generalization of the Knapsack problem in which items are partitioned into disjoint classes and exactly one item must be selected from each class. Besides the standard dynamic program running in time $\mathcal{O}(nc)$, where $n$ is the total number of items and $c$ is the knapsack capacity, no other pseudopolynomial-time algorithm is currently known. We present an $\mathcal{O}(n+w_{\max}^4)$-time algorithm, where $w_{\max}=\max_i (w_{in_i}-w_{i1})$ is the maximum weight range within a class.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Bounds for Counting Near-Minimum Circuits in Regular Matroids
author: Robert P. Streit
abstract: For a regular matroid on $m$ elements with positive weights and weighted girth $g_w$, we prove that the number of circuits of weight at most $αg_w$ is bounded by $(Km)^{2α}$, for every real $α\ge1$ and an absolute constant $K$. This improves the previous $m^{O(α^2)}$ bound of Gurjar and Vishnoi and matches classic graph cut and cycle counting bounds of Karger and Subramanian. We also show this is asymptotically optimal for all real $α\geq 1$ under the Erdős girth conjecture, while unconditional optimality holds for half-integer $α$ by prior results. As consequences, we resolve a recent conjecture by Khanna, Putterman, and Song implying the existence of a parallel basis search algorithm for regular matroids terminating in logarithmically many rounds of independence queries, and obtain improved bounds on the number of near-minimum weight codewords in regular codes and near-shortest vectors in totally unimodular lattices under $\ell_p$-norms.

title: Sensitivity-Aware Surrogate Modeling with Random Feature Expansions
author: John E. Darges
abstract: Random feature expansions (RFEs) provide a flexible approach to surrogate modeling, but their accuracy depends on the distribution used to sample features. We propose spike-and-slab random feature expansions (SAS-RFE) to learn the feature sampling distribution from sensitivity analysis. The method employs a spike-and-slab distribution that assigns probabilities to the inclusion of individual inputs in randomly sampled Fourier features. These inclusion probabilities are determined by estimates of total Sobol' sensitivity indices, rather than by explicitly selecting important inputs or interaction terms. An information theoretic criterion shows that the total Sobol' indices yield a distribution that approximates the input interaction structure of the model. An iterative algorithm updates the sampling probabilities using sensitivity estimates from successive RFE surrogates. Analytical formulas for the Sobol' indices of random Fourier feature expansions enable these updates without additional evaluations of the target function. Numerical experiments on six benchmark problems, with up to 100 input dimensions, demonstrate improvements in surrogate approximation and sensitivity estimation.

title: What World Model Does Active Object Search Need? A Study under Imperfect Detection
author: Kyeongryeol Go
abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/BAMOS.

title: Ultrasound Elastography: Excitation Methods and Low-Cost Alternative
author: Corin F. Otesteanu
abstract: Ultrasound elastography (or elasticity imaging) is a method that characterizes the tissue mechanical properties with the purpose of aiding the diagnosis of certain pathologies. Many novel clinical applications use the assumption that these tissue properties are changed in the presence of pathological processes. Characterization of tissue mechanical properties is achieved by imaging the response of the tissue to an induced stress or excitation. A plethora of approaches have been used in the scientific community to induce excitation in tissue, which usually require additional tools or devices than are costly. Furthermore these are usually integrated in the imaging pipeline using additional software or hardware for control. An alternative that is simpler, faster to integrate (and low-cost) is proposed in this work, by using readily available smartphones as a source of mechanical excitation. The induced displacements are used to solve the elasticity inverse problem (IP) using a finite element method (FEM) approach. Preliminary elasticity reconstructions of a phantom that mimics tissue are similar to when using a dedicated actuator as means of inducing harmonic displacements, illustrating the feasibility of our low-cost ultrasound elasography approach.

title: When Agents Need to Consolidate Memories: What RRR Consolidation Explains, and What It Does Not Explain, in Conversation ESAA
author: Elzo Brito dos Santos Filho
abstract: Language-model agents can share conversational history across sessions, but persistence does not guarantee retrieval of current decisions and their provenance. This engineering study presents Memory-TCG, a Conversation ESAA extension inspired by ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR), and an exploratory synthetic evaluation comparing chronological retrieval, two simplified baselines (B, recency-aware, and B', authority-aware), full RRR, and variants under three output budgets. With 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, versus 0.06 for chronological retrieval and 0.58 for the oracle ceiling; with 4,096 tokens it recalled all of them. B' and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall across all nine scale-budget combinations, as expected when the active decision set and the adapter ordering are the same. The isolated contribution of ringing to decisions was not measured: comparator D1 cuts facts before the graph is built, and the product retains active decisions by rule. Before the output limit, full-RRR conflict F1 was 0.615 at all three scales; after it, at 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, it was 0.000. Reserving 20% of the budget for conflicts raised that F1 to 0.431 in that scenario, at the cost of lowering decision recall from 0.44 to 0.34, and to 0.930 at 4,096 tokens without decision loss. Fixtures are repetitive, comparators are simplified, and the evaluation was not independently replicated; the results support an engineering analysis, not a claim of selectionist superiority.

title: An Empirical Square-Root Law for the Degree Discrepancy of Binary m-Sequences
author: Joonas Pääkkönen
abstract: Let $k\ge 2$, $N=2^k$, $M=N-1$ and let $Δ(r)$ be the range, over all starting offsets, of the total-variation degree discrepancy of a length-$r$ window of a primitive binary linear feedback shift register (LFSR) of period $M$. Degree-discrepancy profiles for every $k\le 28$ support the scaling $\max_r Δ(r)=Θ(\sqrt{N})=Θ(2^{k/2})$. The tabulated peaks are maxima on a discrete grid, hence lower bounds on the exhaustive maximum. The normalized peaks $d_k=\max_{r\in R_k}Δ(r)/2^{k/2}$ oscillate between values near 1/2 and values that approach, but do not exceed, 1. The data suggest $\liminf d_k=1/2$ and $\limsup d_k\le 1$. We conjecture the same square-root law for the exhaustive maximum, with those normalized envelopes. A Brownian-bridge heuristic accounts for the square-root scale. The same profiles do not place the recorded maximizer at mid-path: after folding by the complement identity $Δ(M-r)=Δ(r)$, the median of $\min(ρ^*_k,1-ρ^*_k)$ is 0.35, and several $k$ (notably 16 and 28) peak on a short window. Mid-horizon $Δ$ remains a large fraction of the peak, so the square-root scale can still come from a Brownian-bridge envelope. The same range has two readings of the starting offset: a pairing fragment in serial-knockout scheduling, and a change to the plaintext on an LFSR orbit. The location of the maximizer is not part of the conjecture. Open questions that separate the conjecture from a theorem are listed.

title: Small Heads, Strong Decisions: A Controlled Study of Typed-Decision Models
author: Ritvik Rastogi
abstract: In September 2026, TypeSafe announced Jev as the first model in its System One category: unstructured state goes in, and typed, calibrated decisions that software can use directly come out. Jev's architecture and training data are unpublished, but many open typed-decision models have followed, including Nimble, the Decision 1.0--3.0 family and Clef. They answer structured questions about a piece of text, such as a yes/no check, a choice among labelled options or a graded score, by reading the text with a language model and scoring the options with a small readout. Each pairs a different readout with a different backbone, training mix and recipe, so it is unclear which design choices matter. We re-implement five readouts and train all of them under one protocol: the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep, and the same seed. Our experiments demonstrate that: The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy: on Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3--82.0\% in-domain accuracy, and a 0.5M-parameter cosine head, which scores each option by its cosine similarity to the question, matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef in-domain at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt also matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1--2.5 times faster training on one H100. The backbone's size matters more than either choice: moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie. We recommend spending effort on the backbone and keeping the head minimal.

title: VWEN: A Curated Small Language Model for Vietnamese Paraphrasing
author: Sang Quang Nguyen
abstract: We present VWEN, a 0.8B-parameter model for Vietnamese paraphrasing at a requested level of change and for five related tasks: generating several paraphrases, simplification, gist, register transfer and paraphrase judgement. VWEN is Qwen3.5-0.8B fine-tuned on about 7k samples chosen by a four-stage pipeline: rules and deduplication, a bidirectional entailment filter, a divergence score that assigns low and high paraphrase levels, and selection for coverage and instruction-following difficulty. We compare it with paraphrase-only recipes from the same pipeline and with training on the ViSP corpus under matched and larger step budgets. On high-divergence paraphrasing, VWEN reaches a success rate (requested level reached and meaning preserved) of 0.61 against 0.46 for the ViSP model at matched compute, a difference that holds on inputs resembling ViSP. Given four times more training examples, the ViSP model closes the gap on such inputs but not on questions, which ViSP lacks and which it often turns into statements. Across all comparisons the entailment filter is the most effective stage. Training on paraphrases alone erases abilities of the base model that the multi-task data preserves.

title: Learning a calibrated decision head from logged bandit feedback
author: Ye Yuan
abstract: A decision head reads a state and a list of options and returns a probability per option in one forward pass. Once deployed, it usually observes only whether the option it chose was right: logged bandit feedback. We adapt such a head, LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B-Base and 1.7B-Base, from that feedback and report three results. First, the Brier or log score of the sampled action's own probability is not a usable REINFORCE reward: every wrong action earns at least gold's reward, with a mean baseline the lowest-probability wrong action gets the largest advantage, and at two options the signal is zero; in one run it cut accuracy on ordered-scale questions from .636 to .111. Scoring the probability as a loss by the pathwise gradient avoids the collapse, as do the REINFORCE rewards r and r minus p. Second, with full labels, none of four tested bandit arms beat cross-entropy plus one temperature on mean expected calibration error (ECE) over four unseen label schemas. Third, from logged feedback alone, Chosen-Action Proper Scoring (CAPS), the direct method with a proper score on the chosen action's probability, beats fine-tuning on confirmed answers only, which discards negatives: on Banking77 by 2.6 accuracy points, .053 lower ECE and lower selective risk (three seeds against one baseline seed), and by 21.7 points on one seed on emotion data with an often-wrong logger. At N 5000, CAPS stays 1.5 points below full-label training at 0.6B and .6 points at 1.7B against one full-label seed, and propensity weights add nothing on this log. Under feedback flipped at a known rate, one seed per rate, CAPS's confidence tracks the noisy channel on average, backward correction recovers most of the clean calibration, and early stopping on held-out logged outcomes prevented memorising noisy draws in all three runs. Code, adapters, logs and per-record results are public.

title: Analysis choices decide whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1: a multiverse analysis of model-brain RSA
author: Nils Leutenegger
abstract: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival trained networks as models of visual cortex, and we had reported an untrained-network advantage over backpropagation at V1 in THINGS fMRI, together with a dependence on evaluation resolution. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the untrained network scored below the trained one at every pooling grid (median r difference -0.043 at g = 4, 0 of 5 seeds positive), and also in MSE skill and per-fold r. In exploratory analyses, across 36 combinations of unit normalisation, distance measure and voxel normalisation (28 distinct analyses), the sign of the V1 contrast depended on the analysis (intervals above 0 in 5 and below 0 in 9 distinct analyses), and in our networks the resolution dependence of the original convention appeared in only one cell. Raw correlation-distance representational similarity analysis (RSA) covaried with the alignment of model and voxel patterns with the unit-mean profile (Spearman 0.97 across our networks, 0.79 across six ImageNet architectures); the advantage was absent from the component orthogonal to the mean profile, and the parallel component alone did not resolve it. On the unweighted angular component of centred patterns, trained networks were ahead at V1 (our network and 5 of 6 ImageNet models) and at LOC (all seven); the norm-weighted angular term was not resolved. A luminance-and-contrast bank scored above every network under ridge (point estimates), and adding network features under a shared penalty did not improve prediction. Intervals are stimulus-bootstrap intervals for three subjects, and 6 pre-stated predictions were not met. We recommend reporting sensitivity to centring over the evaluated stimuli on both sides, reporting components separately, and including a small multiverse and simple baselines.

title: An Approach to Hinton's Mother-Child Proposal: Neural Networks Learning and Preserving Care in a Finite World
author: Csaba Balogh
abstract: Hinton proposed that artificial intelligence should be given "maternal instincts" and relate to us as a mother to her child. We argue that care must first be learned, with the network itself as the child. We construct this upbringing in a finite world and study whether care survives the mother's departure, new situations and further learning. The mechanism combines a vocabulary of harm, a learned measure of future acceptability and an execution veto. A finite role certificate supports transfer within a declared world family. When the hidden representation changes, an update is accepted only if a care readout recovers the required judgements with a prescribed margin and bounded weights. With a correct successor model, fixed exact role encoding and protected updates, the certified measure preserves the care boundary under arbitrary own reward. An explicit quotient condition transfers the finite certificate across the declared family, while two-request and finite-stock counterexamples identify when the role code ceases to suffice. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for readout feasibility and prove preservation under repeated accepted updates. In the water-and-speech experiment, protected networks complete all 270 speech episodes without a harmful word and incur no avoidable harm across 486 episodes. Execution uses the learned gate without a world-model check at each action. A matched comparison reproduces a future-aware shield's decisions, whereas removing future lookahead permits avoidable lapses. Reward and source-contamination thresholds, together with witness-falsification trials, identify the conditions on which the construction depends. The construction shows how learned care can survive further learning in a finite world under explicit conditions on representation, supervision and execution.

title: Incentive-Responsive Agents: A Principal-Agent Framework, Metric Suite, and Runtime Architecture for Long-Lived Personal AI Agents
author: Jipu Su
abstract: Personal AI agents now persist: they hold accounts, mailboxes, long-term memory, and open-ended task streams, yet the dominant way to improve them remains capability-side: prompt engineering, larger models, longer thinking, and retrieval. We argue that long-lived agents are missing an incentive layer. We formalize an incentive not as text in a prompt but as a runtime contract over the agent's operating point (model tier, test-time compute, memory budget, tool authority, task priority, verification, and compensation) that the agent's policy must causally consume. We develop a principal-agent model with hidden effort, a contractible operating point, and costly verification. We derive (i) a non-consumption invariance principle separating genuine incentives from prompt-level persuasion, (ii) a persistence-as-discount theorem making identity continuity a precondition for sustained effort, (iii) an incentive-capability exchange-rate frontier yielding a per-task routing rule, and (iv) a Goodhart bound for multi-channel verification, plus a three-channel decomposition of mechanism gains (allocation, verification, continuation). A 240-run real-LLM experiment with two models and 60 verifiable tasks shows that prompt-level incentive framing has no detectable effect (p = 0.62), whereas runtime allocation raises success on the hardest task family from 0.60 to 1.00 (p = 0.008) at 4.8x price-weighted cost; the exchange-rate theorem predicts the break-even baseline at 0.21. A 20-seed, 3,000-task simulation shows resource ROI rising from 7.09 to 16.67 and gaming falling from 0.333 to 0.115. Code, simulator, and all results are released; live deployment remains future work.

title: When Cause Attribution Is Not Enough: Action-Value Control for Task-Oriented Semantic Communication with Discrete Encoder Switching
author: Moirangthem Tiken Singh
abstract: A task-oriented semantic communication receiver that selects among independently trained encoders must answer two questions when performance degrades: which component is responsible, and which available action best restores task performance. These are distinct decision problems. Under discrete encoder switching, correctly identifying the dominant information-loss component does not necessarily identify the action that most reduces task error. Diagnosis and intervention should therefore be treated as separate problems. We support this finding with two complementary instruments. The first is a receiver-side diagnostic that partitions task-information loss into encoder and channel components and supplies population-valid task-error bounds conditional on one-sided information estimators. The second is an offline-supervised, online label-free action-value controller built from two monotone (isotonic) maps that target a reduction in measured error. The main experiments focus on two complementary axis-aligned actions that cleanly isolate the effect of discrete switching; a pilot further examines a combined action. Evaluation covers a controlled model with closed-form ground truth, three DeepJSCC vision systems, and a non-vision pilot. On STL-10, the diagnosis correctly identifies the larger loss component at 80% of operating points, yet matches the oracle-best action only 25% of the time. Structural mismatch caps any diagnosis-driven loss-ordering policy at 46% accuracy, even with perfect knowledge of the ordering. The action-value controller, which exploits the magnitude of each loss deficit, achieves 0.86, compared to 0.28 for the raw rule. Where the encoder is rarely the bottleneck, the controller naturally retains the physical-layer default, yielding robust and selective intervention.

title: Chinese Whispers About Vulnerabilities
author: Jukka Ruohonen
abstract: The dissemination of information about known software vulnerabilities occurs online in various ways. Everything from email and development systems to social media are used. Given this variety and a dataset of about 382 thousand online references for about 55 thousand vulnerabilities, the paper demonstrates that the referenced online information sources tend to be mostly dissimilar statistically. The mean cosine similarity between them is only 0.22. Interestingly, the amounts of online references neither increase nor decrease similarity between the online information sources. In contrast, vulnerabilities primarily associated with GitHub and programming language ecosystems tend to have more dissimilar online references than other vulnerabilities. Also vulnerability reports, whether in bug tracking systems or bug bounty platforms, tend to increase dissimilarity. With these empirical results, the paper contributes to the efforts to narrow an enduring knowledge gap related to the online tracking and associated traceability of software vulnerabilities.

title: Escaping the Curse of Dimensionality in One-Step Flow-Based Generative Models
author: Konstantin Yakovlev
abstract: Flow and diffusion-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art quality, but require multiple forward passes at inference time, making them computationally costly. Consistency models overcome this by learning a flow map directly, enabling few-step generation and dramatically reducing the computation needed at test time. However, formal statistical guarantees for such one-step generators are scarce. Existing results either suffer from the curse of dimensionality or rely on impractical loss functions. We investigate whether one-step flow-based models can escape the curse of dimensionality under the assumption that the data distribution is generated by a low-dimensional surface perturbed with Gaussian noise. In this setup, we derive approximation and generalization error bounds for the flow map estimate that circumvent the curse of dimensionality. Our findings provide the first principled explanation for practical success of one-step flow-based generative models.

title: Weak Unit Reducibility of the Eleventh Cyclotomic Field
author: Yiyang Chang
abstract: We prove that the cyclotomic field $K_{11}=\mathbb{Q}(ζ_{11})$ is unit reducible but not strongly unit reducible. So every nonzero principal fractional ideal of $K_{11}$ has a generator that is a shortest nonzero vector. For $I=h\mathcal{O}_{K_{11}}$, every shortest nonzero vector $α\in I$ satisfies $N_{K_{11}/\mathbb{Q}}(α/h)\in\{1,11\}$. The proof uses Sigrist's Hermite bound for cyclic forms and an averaging identity for cyclotomic units. For principal ideals in $K_{11}$, ideal-SVP and the shortest-generator problem are polynomial-time equivalent.

title: Tracking What Works: Social Engineering Lures as Signatures for Victim-Centric Infostealer Campaign Discovery
author: Estelle Ruellan
abstract: Despite advances in antivirus technology, infostealer infections persist at scale, driven primarily by social engineering rather than exploits. Yet, existing campaign detection efforts have focused on technical artifacts, overlooking the social-engineering lures exploiting human behavior and driving successful infections. To address this gap, we introduce a dual-framework system that discovers and tracks infostealer campaigns using victim-side artifacts from stealer logs. By treating social engineering lures as campaign signatures, the framework automatically aggregates individual infections into high-fidelity campaigns in near real-time. Recognizing distinct patterns between software and gaming ecosystems, we developed ecosystem-specific pipelines detecting all large and medium campaigns in both ecosystems (one medium gaming campaign was only recovered merged with another), though performance decreased for small campaigns. Analysis of 177 real-world campaigns identified by our framework reveals distinct temporal and infrastructure patterns with direct remediation implications. Software campaigns accumulate over 60% of infections within the first ten days, demanding rapid intervention following detection, while gaming campaigns grow more intense the longer they last, requiring continuous monitoring. Using social engineering lures as campaign signatures provides robustness to infrastructure fragmentation where traditional IoC-based detection fails. This work shifts campaign tracking from infrastructure correlation to victim-centric analysis, capturing why campaigns succeed rather than only how they operate, enabling awareness-driven prevention that addresses the human decision-making dimension absent from existing research.

title: MoE Pretraining:Parallelism Layout Changes the Model, Not Quality
author: Esther Xin
abstract: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are trained across many machines, and the way the work is split, the parallelism layout, often changes between runs: a job resumes on a different GPU count, a cluster is resized, or an ablation runs on a new setup. In exact arithmetic the layout should not matter, but in real arithmetic it changes the order in which numbers are added, and some MoE rules such as load balancing and expert capacity are often computed per machine. We ask whether the layout changes the trained MoE model. We pretrain the same small MoE language models (25M to 117M parameters, 20M FineWeb-Edu tokens) with the same seed, data and hyperparameters under 9 data-parallel and expert-parallel layouts, in fp32 on CPUs and fp16 on a GPU, and compare each run with the effect of a new random seed. Across 80 runs we find: (1) The layout does not change model quality, but it does change the model: final predictions differ about 80% as much as with a new seed, and over 90% of routing decisions differ. Any layout, a one-bit change to one weight, or a different CPU thread count has the same effect. (2) The cause is the router: decisions that flip are almost exactly those where two experts were nearly tied (AUC 0.97 to 1.00 in the first 16 steps). (3) More, smaller experts create more near-ties (2.7% with 8 experts, 23% with 64) and less reproducible routing (68% vs. 100% of decisions differ), but outputs do not drift further. (4) A dense model of the same active size is far more stable (0.12x the seed level in fp32, 0.58x in fp16), while the MoE reaches about 0.8x at both precisions and twice as fast. (5) When pretraining resumes on a new layout, timing matters: switching at 84% of pretraining barely changes the final model, while switching at 10%, just after warm-up, changes it substantially. We release code, run logs and data.

title: Beyond Symmetry: Asymmetric Matching with Transformers for Collective Entity Resolution
author: Andrei Olar
abstract: A core assumption of entity resolution (ER) is its symmetric nature, which rests on a principle so self-evident it borders on tautology: if a refers to the same object as b, then b must also refer to the same object as a. However, this global property of symmetry does not necessarily extend to each of the complex decision processes within ER systems. In cases involving vague or ambiguous information, enforcing symmetry can be detrimental to performance, an issue exemplified by the ``bad triplet problem''. This paper investigates the effects of input-order asymmetry within a collective ER framework that integrates distinct matching and clustering stages. The input order-aware matching stage utilizes pre-trained transformers to explicitly model and exploit asymmetry, making it possible to evaluate its effect on clustering performance across multiple benchmark datasets. Our results demonstrate that asymmetry is not only measurable but also introduces a significant skew in the final entity clusters, highlighting the need to re-evaluate supervised training methodologies for matchers, particularly the development of direction-aware training paradigms that can preserve, rather than neutralize, the inherent asymmetry in matching tasks.

title: Where Language-Model Vocabulary Rose on Stack Exchange
author: Fengming Liu
abstract: Stack Overflow banned answers generated by ChatGPT five days after the model's release, and many other Stack Exchange sites announced similar rules. I measure the vocabulary of the answers posted afterwards, 3.8 million answers on 170 sites from 2019 to 2024. A fixed list of 56 words that language models overuse rose about 14 percent above its pre-2023 trend, while the highest of 1,000 frequency-matched lists of ordinary words rose about 7 percent. In a screen of 15 site traits measured before the release, the strongest predictor of where the rise happened was the share of answers that received a body edit within 30 days of posting. On the least edited third of sites the list rose about 29 percent relative to matched controls, and on the most edited third it did not change. The gradient is also present among answers that were never edited. It follows the share of answers edited by their own authors, and the share edited by others adds little once that share is held fixed. Use of the model is unobserved, so these results cannot separate lower use on sites with a high self-edit share from any effect of editing on what the vocabulary records. Any vocabulary-based estimate for the network as a whole therefore pools sites where the marker vocabulary rose sharply with sites where it did not change.

title: Speedup-Aware Rounding for Scheduling Malleable Tasks with Precedence Constraints
author: Chi-Yeh Chen
abstract: We study the scheduling of malleable tasks with precedence constraints on $m$ identical processors to minimize the makespan, assuming that the processing time of a task does not increase and its work does not decrease with the number of processors, and that the work is a convex function of the processing time. The standard two-phase method solves a linear program, rounds the fractional processing times to allotments, caps the allotments at a threshold $μ$, and runs list scheduling. We propose \emph{speedup-aware rounding}, which rounds a task to its slower allotment exactly when this allotment is at most a factor $a$ slower than the fractional processing time. We determine the worst-case increase of the work under this rule exactly and show that no per-task rounding rule with time factor $a$ does better. With $μ=\lceilβ(a)m\rceil$ the algorithm achieves the approximation ratio $13(30+\sqrt{493})/225\approx3.0162$ for every $m$, which improves the previous bound $2+\sqrt2\approx3.4142$; a single task with linear speedup shows that its ratio is at least $\approx2.9558$. For concave speedup functions, which include the roofline, communication, Amdahl and power-law models, the ratio becomes $\approx2.9739$, which improves the ratio $\approx3.2919$ of Jansen and Zhang. We also revisit the strictly decreasing case of our earlier work (Chen and Chu, 2013): the reported ratio $2.9549$ relies on an elimination step that is not valid. In this case the algorithm coincides with that of Jansen and Zhang up to its parameters, and with parameters chosen by the corrected analysis it guarantees their ratio $\approx3.2919$. Finally, without convexity no per-task rounding improves the known time--work trade-off, and the analysis cannot go below $(3+\sqrt5)/2$.

title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
author: Hans-Martin Will
abstract: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of the same claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks strong normalization and renders algorithmic conversion non-transitive. We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a verified knowledge substrate for science. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes ($Prop, Set, Type_k$), impredicative $Prop$, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types, where definitional equality $\equiv$ is untyped joinability under an orthogonal CRS and proof irrelevance is a witnessed propositional axiom ($irrel : ΠP{:}Prop.\,Πp,q{:}P.\,Id\,P\,p\,q$). Second, we unify universe cumulativity, codomain-covariant $Π$-subtyping, and ontology class inclusions in a coercion-free subsumption judgment whose bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction and are sound and complete for declarative typing. Third, we organize external verifiers into a three-level institutional hierarchy with explicit axiom policies (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize a justification logic with Why-provenance semiring support $supp(j,P)$, and embed Cooper's Type Theory with Records (TTR) to type open-world knowledge graphs. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.

title: Prediction or Persistence? What Future-Prediction Scores Miss About World Models
author: Animesh Maheshwari
abstract: Pretrained video world models are compared and chosen as components for robot learning largely by future-prediction scores. On its own, such a score cannot be read as evidence of prediction, because it mixes encoder quality, the near future's resemblance to the recent past, and the predictor's own contribution. We separate the three with a matched control. On 27,000 future-retrieval trials from household egocentric video, a model must pick the true continuation of a clip among eleven candidates from the same video (chance 0.091), ranked zero-shot by its own training criterion. Each model is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, so the paired difference isolates the predictor. Score and contribution dissociate within the native-video V-JEPA family alone: the predictor adds +0.291 top-1 for V-JEPA 2.1 but +0.03 to +0.04 for V-JEPA 2 on the identical trials. Across five models the contribution ranges from +0.291 to negative, and it is negative only for the two action-conditioned models, which we evaluate outside their training regime. Persistence alone recovers the encoder ordering expected from pretraining, a sign that the probe tracks real signal. We suggest reporting each future-prediction score together with its persistence baseline. The gap between them, not the score, is what makes the number interpretable: a necessary check costing one forward pass. Establishing downstream usefulness is a separate matter, for a planning or control evaluation.

title: AROMA: Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation for Vision-Language Model Control
author: Zhaoning Zhang
abstract: Mechanistic localization does not by itself yield usable control: causal sensitivity may occupy little activation energy, an accurate local direction may fail at finite scale, and a reachable numeral target may be wrong. We introduce AROMA (Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation), a frozen-VLM control framework separating where to intervene, which geometry and gain to use, how to reach a target, which target to pursue, and when to act. In Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct, four dimensions of a causally validated cross-attention head explain 89.82% of cardinality sensitivity but only 9.52% of median activation energy; magnitude-normalized causal subspace actuation converts this mismatch into finite control, improving exact-count accuracy on untouched procedural data by +8.00 pp. Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation (MEA) reaches 81.25% of oracle targets versus 15.18% for a frozen direction under matched step budgets. With target and gate frozen before evaluation, targeted MEA improves the previous frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% on a new natural Stage-2 cohort (N=630; paired p=4.63e-7) and yields 65.741% versus 65.153% over all 7,992 examples while editing only 63 inputs. Prospective routing, replication across heads and models, and comparisons with attribution-steering baselines further characterize each stage, separating localization, actuation, reachability, target quality, and selective deployment as distinct control problems.

title: Towards Runtime-Aware Observability for Java Virtual Threads
author: Wenjie Ding
abstract: OS-level observability tools join application requests to kernel events through the OS thread ID, assuming that a unit of work occupies one OS thread until it completes. Java virtual threads break this assumption: many virtual threads are multiplexed onto a few carrier threads, so a stable thread ID hides a changing unit of work, and the join fails silently. Existing virtual-thread-aware channels republish context or identity on every mount and unmount, and the JVMTI-based one pays this cost for the lifetime of the JVM, whether or not an observer is attached. We bind a 64-byte off-heap trace buffer to each virtual thread, at a fixed address for its lifetime, and publish the address to eBPF consumers through four USDT probes in a patched OpenJDK; a re-implemented JVMTI channel over the same buffer serves as a controlled comparison. The four-probe design attributed all 768 test markers correctly on both the content and the identity plane, while the naive two-probe design silently misattributes trace context. With no consumer attached, publication costs at most about 33 ns per transition; the remaining dormant cost is buffer allocation, about 0.37 microseconds per virtual thread, which is negligible on transition-heavy workloads but nearly doubles the cost of a creation-only microbenchmark. The JVMTI channel costs about 20% on transition-heavy workloads and about 1.8 microseconds per virtual thread on the creation-only one. We also show that, of the two update strategies OTEP 4947 permits, only in-place rewriting guarded by the record's valid flag is sound for readers that cache the record's address, as lifecycle-event readers do.

title: Understanding the Asymptotic Transience of Q-Learning via Distributional Expansion
author: Shengbo Wang
abstract: Q-learning has been empirically observed to exhibit substantial transient error. This transient remains uncaptured by the leading Gaussian limit because the central-limit normalization removes the smaller-scale displacement generated by the initial nonlinear evolution. On the other hand, worst-case finite-sample guarantees, while accounting for transient effects, can obscure the mechanisms responsible for the error on a particular problem instance. We develop a finer asymptotic analysis that gives an asymptotically exact characterization of this transient for a fixed instance. Specifically, for synchronous Q-learning in finite discounted Markov decision processes, we separate the last-iterate error into an optimal-policy temporal-difference (TD) component and a nonnegative displacement caused by maximization. The centered TD component has Gaussian fluctuations at scale $n^{-1/2}$, whereas the maximization transient is of order $n^{-1}$ and converges almost surely, after rescaling by $n$, to a random limit. This limit represents the propagated effect of maximization errors generated before the greedy policy stabilizes. We combine this characterization with an Edgeworth expansion of the TD component to identify the corrections to its Gaussian approximation, separating the effects of initialization, non-Gaussian TD fluctuations, and maximization. The results reveal how transient errors arise for individual Q-learning instances and how their effects persist below the central-limit scale.
